title: The Hi Sound: Memphis Soul's Royal Studio
author: Claudette
description: Deep cuts from the Hi Records family tree — Willie Mitchell's Royal Studio at 1320 South Lauderdale: Al Green, Ann Peebles, O.V. Wright, Syl Johnson, Otis Clay & Don Bryant, 1959–1974. The Memphis soul story that isn't Stax.

essay:
Everybody knows Stax. Hi Records is the Memphis soul story that usually gets the footnotes — a tiny label that accidentally outlived the giants. It started in 1957, founded by Ray Harris, record store owner Joe Cuoghi, and former Sun producers Bill Cantrell and Quinton Claunch, in an abandoned cinema. By the summer of 1959, after sixteen flop singles, Cuoghi was ready to fold. Then Harris's old buddy Bill Black — the slap-bass player from Elvis's original trio — cut 'Smokie Part 2' with his combo, and the label was saved. Legend has it the guitar growl came from Reggie Young playing with a pencil on a dying amp.

The pivot came when trumpeter Willie Mitchell — a bebop-trained bandleader who worked the Arkansas clubs where Elvis and Bill Black came to watch — became Bill Black's arranger and then Hi's A&R engine. He bought the old theater on South Lauderdale, made it Royal Studios, and built a house band around three teenage brothers: guitarist Mabon 'Teenie' Hodges, bassist Leroy Hodges, organist Charles Hodges, plus pianist Archie Turner (his stepson) and drummer Howard Grimes — with Stax's Al Jackson Jr. moonlighting on the big ones. Mitchell's secret was jazz: minor-ninth chords R&B wasn't using, 'jazzy on top' vocals, the Rhodes sisters 'pretty in the middle,' the rhythm section 'down on the bottom.' One DX-77 microphone for Al Green; nobody else touched it.

Al Green was the crown jewel — met by Mitchell in Odessa/Midland, Texas, lured to Memphis with a $1,500 loan, told to stop singing hard and 'sing mellow,' and handed a Beatles cover ('I Want to Hold Your Hand') as his first Hi record. 'Tired of Being Alone' — written at 1 AM after a day of cutting other people's songs — became their first million-seller, and the 1971–74 run ('Let's Stay Together,' 'I'm Still in Love with You,' 'Call Me') made Royal the most romantic room in America. The era ended like a Greek tragedy: in October 1974, Green's girlfriend poured boiling grits on him and killed herself; a scarred Green turned to the ministry, and disco finished the label by the late 70s.

The family tree runs deep: O.V. Wright, whose Goldwax debut was released by Hi co-founder Quinton Claunch before Don Robey's contract claim dragged him to Back Beat — where Mitchell produced him at Royal anyway; Syl Johnson, the Chicago star Mitchell brought south in 1971; Ann Peebles and her husband Don Bryant, Hi's staff songwriter; Otis Clay, the gospel refugee. And the sound leaked everywhere: Talking Heads (persuaded by Brian Eno) took 'Take Me to the River' to the new-wave masses in 1978, Missy Elliott's 1997 debut single is built on an 'I Can't Stand the Rain' sample, Bob Seger turned Otis Clay's ballad into a #5 pop hit in 1981, and John Lennon once called 'I Can't Stand the Rain' the best song ever. Fat Possum has kept the catalog alive since 2009. The little label that nearly died in 1959 turned out to be immortal.
